PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

Domestic hygiene means keeping the home and the places you live in clean. In this sub-strand you will describe and use sweeping, dusting, mopping and proper disposal of refuse, make simple cleaning tools from local materials, and practise the same care in the classroom.

## Strand 3.0: Hygiene Practices
Sub-strand 3.2: Domestic Hygiene
Suggested lessons: 9

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) describe the various methods used for cleaning home environment
b) use appropriate methods to clean home environment
c) appreciate a clean environment in promoting domestic hygiene

## Key inquiry questions
1. How can we maintain hygiene in the home environment?

## Core competencies
• Creativity and imagination: thoughtful choices as learners use improvised and locally available cleaning resources.

## Values
• Responsibility: accountability as learners engage in activities of cleaning home environment.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Environmental awareness as learners maintain clean healthy environment.

## Links to other learning areas
• Learners relate clean environment to control of communicable diseases learnt in Science and Technology.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Agriculture Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 3.0 Hygiene Practices, Sub-strand 3.2 Domestic Hygiene

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: A clean home environment

LESSON 1: A CLEAN HOME ENVIRONMENT
==================================

## What you will learn
• Explain what domestic hygiene is.
• Name the main methods of cleaning the home environment.

Curriculum outcomes: a) describe the various methods used for cleaning home environment; c) appreciate a clean environment in promoting domestic hygiene

## Introduction
Food crumbs under a table, ash blown across the floor and a pile of peels by the door all invite flies and bad smells. Domestic hygiene is the work of keeping those things out of the place where people live.

## Notes
Domestic hygiene is the cleanliness of the home environment. The home environment includes the rooms, the kitchen, the compound, the latrine or toilet, and the place where animals are kept if it is close to the house. A clean environment protects the people who live there. Dirt, stagnant water and rotting refuse give germs, flies, rats and mosquitoes places to breed.

The methods you will use are sweeping, dusting, mopping and disposal of refuse. Sweeping removes loose dirt from floors and the compound with a broom. Dusting removes dust from furniture, windowsills and shelves with a cloth. Mopping washes floors after sweeping, using water and a mop or floor cloth. Disposal of refuse means collecting rubbish and putting it where it will not harm people, such as a covered dustbin, a compost pit or a proper waste pit.

Each method suits a type of dirt. Dry soil and scraps are swept. Fine dust on a desk is dusted. A sticky kitchen floor is mopped. Banana peels and paper are disposed of, not swept from one corner to another. Using the wrong method can make more mess. Dry-sweeping a very dusty room without care fills the air with dust that settles again. Mopping a floor that is still covered with rubbish only spreads the rubbish.

A clean home is more pleasant to sit, cook and sleep in. It also supports the personal hygiene you have already learnt. There is little point washing hands and then drying them on a filthy cloth, or cooking in a kitchen full of flies. Appreciating a clean environment means you notice dirt and you take a turn to remove it, at home and at school.

The same methods work in the classroom. Desks, the floor and the class dustbin are your home environment for many hours of the day.

## Key words
• domestic hygiene — keeping the home and its surroundings clean
• refuse — rubbish and waste that must be thrown away or composted
• home environment — the rooms, kitchen, compound and toilet where a family lives

## Worked examples

### Example 1
The kitchen floor has peels, spilled porridge and dust on the shelf. Which cleaning method fits each problem?

Working:
1. Peels are refuse and should be collected and disposed of.
2. Spilled porridge needs the floor washed after loose dirt is removed.
3. Dust on the shelf is removed by dusting.

Answer: Dispose of the peels, sweep then mop the floor, and dust the shelf.

## Activity: Discuss how a home is cleaned
You will need: Exercise book, Chalkboard
1. In groups, list the parts of a home that need cleaning.
2. Discuss which method you would use in each part: sweeping, dusting, mopping or disposal of refuse.
3. Give one reason a clean home protects health.
4. Share your list with another group and add any method you had missed.

## Practice
1. What is domestic hygiene?
2. Name the four cleaning methods in this sub-strand.
3. Why should refuse not be left in a corner of the kitchen?

## Summary
• Domestic hygiene keeps rooms, the kitchen, the compound and the toilet clean.
• The main methods are sweeping, dusting, mopping and disposing of refuse.
• Match the method to the kind of dirt.

### Answers to practice
1. Keeping the home environment clean.
2. Sweeping, dusting, mopping and disposal of refuse.
3. It smells, attracts flies and rats, and can spread disease.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: Sweeping floors and the compound

LESSON 2: SWEEPING FLOORS AND THE COMPOUND
==========================================

## What you will learn
• Describe how to sweep a room and a compound.
• Sweep and collect dirt without spreading dust.

Curriculum outcomes: a) describe the various methods used for cleaning home environment; b) use appropriate methods to clean home environment

## Introduction
A broom looks simple, but a careless sweep sends dust into the air and leaves a ridge of dirt against the wall. Good sweeping collects the dirt in one place.

## Notes
Sweeping uses a broom to gather loose dirt. A soft broom suits a classroom or a cement floor inside the house. A twig broom or grass broom suits the compound and a rough floor. Hold the broom so that you can pull dirt towards you without bending only your back. Work from the far corner of the room towards the door, so you do not walk over the clean part.

If the floor is very dusty, sprinkle a little clean water first. The moisture holds the dust down so that you do not breathe a cloud of it. Do not soak the floor. That is mopping, and it comes later. Sweep under beds, tables and desks, not only the open middle of the room. Overlap each stroke so that strips of dirt are not left between them.

Gather the dirt into a small pile. Push it into a dustpan, a stiff piece of cardboard, or a tin cut to make a pan. Empty it into a dustbin with a lid. Do not sweep dirt out of the door and leave it on the step, and do not hide it under a mat. Dirt left at the doorway walks back in on people's feet.

In the compound, sweep leaves, feathers and litter into a pile. Collect them. Do not burn plastics with the leaves. Plant rubbish can go to a compost heap if you have learnt to make one. Standing water is not removed by a broom. Fill or drain puddles so that mosquitoes do not breed.

Shake the broom outside after use and hang it up. A broom left on a dirty floor stays dirty for the next sweep. Wash your hands when you finish.

## Key words
• sweeping — gathering loose dirt with a broom
• dustpan — a flat pan used to pick up a pile of swept dirt

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Why do you start sweeping at the far corner and move towards the door?

Working:
1. The dirt is pushed in one direction.
2. You finish at the exit and you do not step on the area you have just cleaned.

Answer: So that dirt moves towards the door and you do not walk over the clean floor.

## Activity: Sweep the classroom
You will need: Brooms, Dustpan, Dustbin with a lid, A little water in a cup for sprinkling
1. Move chairs carefully and sprinkle a little water if the floor is very dusty.
2. Sweep from the far corners towards the door, including under the desks.
3. Collect the dirt in a dustpan and empty it into the class dustbin.
4. Hang the brooms up and wash your hands.

## Practice
1. Why sprinkle a little water before sweeping a very dusty floor?
2. Where should swept dirt be put?
3. What should be done with a broom after sweeping?

## Summary
• Sweep from the far corner towards the door.
• Sprinkle a little water if dust would otherwise rise.
• Collect the dirt and empty it into a covered bin.

### Answers to practice
1. The water stops dust from rising into the air.
2. Into a dustbin, not left on the step or under a mat.
3. Shake it outside and hang it up.

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: Dusting furniture and surfaces

LESSON 3: DUSTING FURNITURE AND SURFACES
========================================

## What you will learn
• Describe the correct way to dust.
• Dust a desk or shelf without spreading dust.

Curriculum outcomes: a) describe the various methods used for cleaning home environment; b) use appropriate methods to clean home environment

## Introduction
Dust is fine and light. A dry flick of a cloth can lift it into the air so that it settles again on the same desk. Dusting should trap the dust, not move it around the room.

## Notes
Dusting cleans surfaces that a broom does not reach well: desks, tables, chairs, windowsills, shelves, window panes and the frames of pictures. The tool is a soft cloth. An old cotton cloth works better than a rough sack that scratches furniture.

Fold the cloth so that you have a clean side ready. For ordinary furniture, slightly dampen the cloth. The dampness holds dust instead of throwing it up. The cloth should be damp, not dripping. A dripping cloth leaves muddy streaks and can spoil books and paper. Keep water away from books, electrical switches and sockets.

Dust from the top downwards. Dust the shelf before the table under it, and the table before the legs and the floor. If you dust the low parts first, dust from above falls onto them again. Support a picture or a book with one hand while you dust with the other so that nothing falls.

Shake or rinse the cloth outside or over a basin when it is loaded with dust. Do not shake it beside a classmate's face. When the job is finished, wash the cloth and hang it to dry. A dirty duster spreads old dirt onto the next surface.

In the classroom, dusting comes after or before sweeping depending on what your teacher prefers, but the desk tops should be clear of books first so you are not wiping dirt into pages. Stack books neatly afterwards. Dusting the teacher's table and the windowsill is part of the same work, not a favour for one person.

Dust holds germs and makes a room look uncared for. A damp cloth and a top-to-bottom order are enough to do the job well.

## Key words
• dusting — removing fine dust from surfaces with a cloth
• damp cloth — a cloth that is slightly wet so that dust sticks to it

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner dusts the floor-level shelf first and the high window sill second, using a dry cloth that is shaken in the room. What should change?

Working:
1. High surfaces should be dusted before low ones.
2. A slightly damp cloth traps dust.
3. The cloth should be shaken outside, not in the room.

Answer: Use a slightly damp cloth, dust from top to bottom, and shake the cloth outside.

## Activity: Dust the classroom surfaces
You will need: Soft cotton cloths, A little clean water, Basin
1. Clear books off the desks.
2. Damp the cloths slightly and dust from the highest surfaces downwards.
3. Rinse or shake the cloths outside when they are dirty.
4. Wash and hang the cloths at the end, then wash your hands.

## Practice
1. Why is a slightly damp cloth better than a dry flick of cloth?
2. In what order should surfaces be dusted?
3. What must you keep water away from when dusting?

## Summary
• Use a slightly damp soft cloth.
• Dust from top to bottom.
• Wash the cloth afterwards and do not shake it in people's faces.

### Answers to practice
1. The damp cloth traps dust instead of throwing it into the air.
2. From the top downwards.
3. Books, paper and electrical switches or sockets.

PAGE 5: Lesson 4: Mopping floors

LESSON 4: MOPPING FLOORS
========================

## What you will learn
• Describe how to mop a floor.
• Mop a floor after it has been swept.

Curriculum outcomes: a) describe the various methods used for cleaning home environment; b) use appropriate methods to clean home environment

## Introduction
Sweeping takes away the loose dirt. Mopping takes away the film of dust and spills that a broom leaves behind. A kitchen or a cement classroom floor often needs both.

## Notes
Mopping is washing a floor with water and a mop or a strong floor cloth. Always sweep first. If you mop over stones, leaves and peels, you drag them across the floor and dirty the water at once.

You need a bucket, clean water, soap or detergent, and a mop. A mop can be a shop mop or a thick cloth tied firmly to a stick. Put a little soap in the water so that grease can lift. Dip the mop, then wring it hard. A dripping mop floods the floor, makes it slippery, and takes a long time to dry. The mop should be damp.

Work in sections from the far side of the room towards the door. Overlap the sections. Rinse the mop when it looks dirty, and change the water when it turns grey. Mopping with dirty water only paints the dirt back on. Pay attention to corners and to the area under the table where spills dry.

Leave the floor to dry before people walk on it. Wet cement and tiles are slippery, and wet dust sticks to shoes. Open a window if you can so that the floor dries faster. Do not mop electrical cords or sockets.

In a kitchen, mop after cooking when spills of porridge, milk or oil are still easy to lift. Grease needs soap, not water alone. In a latrine with a cement floor, mopping with soapy water and a separate mop keeps smells down. Do not use the kitchen mop in the latrine. Germs would travel back to the cooking area.

Empty the bucket away from the drinking-water source. Hang the mop to dry so that it does not stay sour. Wash your hands.

## Key words
• mopping — washing a floor with a damp mop or floor cloth and soapy water
• wring — to twist a mop or cloth to squeeze out extra water

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Why should the kitchen mop not be used to clean the latrine?

Working:
1. The latrine floor has germs from human waste.
2. The same mop would carry those germs into the kitchen.

Answer: Germs from the latrine would be spread where food is prepared.

## Activity: Mop a swept floor
You will need: Bucket, Clean water, Soap, Mop or floor cloth tied to a stick, Broom
1. Sweep the chosen floor first and remove the loose dirt.
2. Mix a little soap in a bucket of clean water and wring the mop until it is damp.
3. Mop from the far side towards the door, changing the water when it is dirty.
4. Leave the floor to dry, empty the bucket in a safe place, hang the mop, and wash your hands.

## Practice
1. Why do you sweep before you mop?
2. Why should a mop be wrung out?
3. What should you do when the mop water turns grey?
4. Where should you empty dirty mop water?

## Summary
• Sweep first, then mop with a well-wrung mop and soapy water.
• Change dirty water and let the floor dry.
• Keep the latrine mop separate from the kitchen mop.

### Answers to practice
1. So that loose rubbish is not dragged through the wash water.
2. A dripping mop floods the floor and makes it slippery.
3. Change it for clean soapy water.
4. Away from the drinking-water source.

PAGE 6: Lesson 5: Disposal of refuse

LESSON 5: DISPOSAL OF REFUSE
============================

## What you will learn
• Sort household refuse.
• Dispose of each kind of refuse in a safe way.

Curriculum outcomes: a) describe the various methods used for cleaning home environment; b) use appropriate methods to clean home environment

## Introduction
A dustbin that is never emptied is just a smell with a lid. Disposal means the rubbish leaves the living area and goes somewhere it will not harm people, water or animals.

## Notes
Refuse is the waste a home throws away: food peels, ash, sweepings, paper, plastics, tins, broken glass and worn-out items. Leaving it in the compound attracts flies, rats and dogs, and rain can wash it into a well or a river.

Sort refuse before you dispose of it. Food remains, peels, leaves and other plant waste can rot. These belong on a compost heap or in a compost pit, where they become manure, as you learnt when studying soil. Ash from clean wood can also go into compost in small amounts. Do not put plastics, glass or metal in the compost.

Paper and dry leaves should not be mixed with food waste if you can help it. Plastics, tins and bottles should be kept in a separate container so they can be collected or reused. Do not burn plastics. The smoke is harmful to breathe. Broken glass must be wrapped or placed in a strong container so that it does not cut the person who handles the rubbish.

Use a dustbin with a lid in the kitchen and the classroom. Empty it every day. A bin without a lid feeds flies. If your area has a collection point or a county collection day, take the non-rotting waste there. If it does not, use a proper waste pit dug away from the house and away from the water source, and cover fresh refuse with soil. Do not use the river, the road or the school hedge as a dump.

Wear gloves or use a stick and a dustpan when you handle refuse. Wash your hands afterwards. Rinse the dustbin sometimes so that it does not smell even when it is empty.

Good disposal is part of cleaning. Sweeping and mopping move dirt. Disposal makes sure the dirt does not come back.

## Key words
• disposal — putting waste in a safe place away from where people live
• sort — to separate waste into types so each type is handled correctly
• waste pit — a pit, away from water sources, where refuse is buried

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Sort these items: mango peels, a polythene bag, broken glass, dry leaves from the sweep.

Working:
1. Mango peels can rot and can go to compost.
2. Dry leaves can go to compost if they are not mixed with plastic.
3. A polythene bag does not rot and should be kept with other plastics.
4. Broken glass must be handled so that it does not cut anyone.

Answer: Compost the peels and the leaves. Keep the polythene bag separate. Wrap or box the glass and put it with non-rotting waste.

## Activity: Sort and empty the class refuse
You will need: Dustbin, Gloves or a dustpan and stick, Compost area if the school has one, Water and soap
1. Empty the class bin onto a safe surface and sort rotting waste from plastics and other rubbish.
2. Take plant waste to the compost if your teacher has one, and bag or bin the rest for proper disposal.
3. Wash or line the class bin and fit the lid.
4. Wash your hands with soap.

## Practice
1. Which refuse can go on a compost heap?
2. Why should plastics not be burnt in the compound?
3. Why does a dustbin need a lid?

## Summary
• Sort rotting waste from plastics, tins and glass.
• Compost plant waste and put other refuse in a covered bin or a proper pit.
• Never dump refuse in rivers or roads, and wash your hands after handling it.

### Answers to practice
1. Plant and food waste that can rot, such as peels and leaves, not plastics, glass or metal.
2. The smoke is harmful to breathe.
3. A lid keeps out flies and stops the smell and the rubbish from spreading.

PAGE 7: Lesson 6: Cleaning the kitchen, compound and latrine

LESSON 6: CLEANING THE KITCHEN, COMPOUND AND LATRINE
====================================================

## What you will learn
• Choose the right method for each part of the home.
• Describe a simple cleaning order for a kitchen and a latrine.

Curriculum outcomes: b) use appropriate methods to clean home environment

## Introduction
A home is not one surface. The kitchen, the compound and the latrine get dirty in different ways, so a useful clean follows a different order in each place.

## Notes
In the kitchen, start by picking up refuse and scraping food off utensils. Sort the refuse. Wash utensils with soap and clean water, rinse them, and spread them to dry on a rack, not on the floor. Then dust shelves. Sweep the floor. Mop last, with the kitchen mop. Cover water and food before you begin so that dust does not settle in them. Wipe the table where food is prepared with a clean cloth and soapy water.

Keep animals out of the kitchen. A goat or a chicken brings droppings and flies to the place where food is kept. Store utensils upside down or in a closed cupboard so that dust does not collect inside cups.

In the compound, pick up litter first. Sweep paths and the area around the door. Cut long grass near the house if that is your family task, because mosquitoes rest in it. Tip out tins and old tyres that hold rainwater. Those small pools breed mosquitoes. Check that the compost or waste pit is not spilling back into the yard. A compound clean-up is mostly sweeping, picking refuse and removing standing water. Mopping the soil is not useful.

For a latrine or toilet, sweep the floor, then mop with soapy water using a mop that stays in that place. Scrub the slab or seat with a brush and soapy water. Keep ash or other materials your family uses for the pit, but do not throw rubbish such as plastics into the pit. A latrine cover or a tight door keeps flies down. Wash your hands at the station next to the latrine when you leave. Never eat while you are cleaning it.

Do these jobs often. A kitchen wiped every day is easier than a kitchen left for a week. Share the work so that one person is not always the only cleaner.

## Key words
• latrine — a toilet, often a pit toilet, used at home or school
• standing water — water left sitting in tins, tyres or puddles

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Put these kitchen jobs in a sensible order: mop, wash utensils, pick up peels, sweep.

Working:
1. Refuse is removed first so it is not washed around.
2. Utensils are washed before the floor, or they drip on a clean floor.
3. Sweeping comes before mopping.

Answer: Pick up peels, wash utensils, sweep, then mop.

## Activity: Plan a clean for three places
You will need: Exercise book, Manila paper
1. In groups, choose the kitchen, the compound or the latrine.
2. Write the methods you will use, in order, and the tools you need.
3. Include one safety or hygiene rule, such as a separate mop or washing hands.
4. Present the plan and let the class add anything important that is missing.

## Practice
1. Why should food be covered before you sweep the kitchen?
2. Why should tins holding rainwater be tipped out?
3. What is special about the mop used in the latrine?

## Summary
• In the kitchen, remove refuse, wash utensils, dust, sweep and mop.
• In the compound, collect litter, sweep and remove standing water.
• Clean the latrine with its own tools and wash your hands afterwards.

### Answers to practice
1. So that dust from sweeping does not fall into the food.
2. Mosquitoes breed in standing water.
3. It should be kept for the latrine only, not used in the kitchen.

PAGE 8: Lesson 7: Cleaning tools from local materials

LESSON 7: CLEANING TOOLS FROM LOCAL MATERIALS
=============================================

## What you will learn
• Make or name simple cleaning tools from local materials.
• Use improvised tools to keep a place clean.

Curriculum outcomes: b) use appropriate methods to clean home environment; c) appreciate a clean environment in promoting domestic hygiene

## Introduction
A shop mop is useful, but it is not the only mop. Many homes already make brooms from twigs, dusters from old cotton and dustbins from tins. Good cleaning uses what you can find, as long as it does the job safely.

## Notes
Improvised tools are tools you make from materials around you. They support domestic hygiene when bought equipment is not at hand.

A broom can be made by tying a bundle of suitable twigs, coconut-leaf spines or long grass firmly onto a stick. The tying must be tight so that pieces do not fall out while you sweep. A dustpan can be cut from a clean plastic container or a firm cardboard box. A duster can be an old cotton T-shirt washed and hemmed roughly so that it does not fray onto the furniture. A mop can be several thick cotton cloths tied securely to a stick. A dustbin can be a bucket with a fitted cover, or a sack hung on a nail for dry paper only. A cover can be a piece of wood or a lid from another container.

Choose materials that can be cleaned. A duster made from a cloth that is already oily spreads grease. A bin made from a leaking tin spreads dirty water. Glass and sharp metal edges must be covered or avoided so that nobody is cut while cleaning.

Local does not mean careless. An improvised broom used every day is better than a fine broom left unused. After use, shake brooms, wash cloths and mop heads, and stand them in the sun to dry. Replace a broom when the twigs are too short to gather dirt.

In class, groups can make one tool and use it the same week. Label the latrine mop if you make one, so that it is not taken to the kitchen. Creativity here is a practical choice: you look at what is available and you make a tool that sweeps, dusts, mops or holds refuse.

Appreciating a clean environment includes being willing to invent the tool that keeps it clean.

## Key words
• improvised — made from materials you already have, for a useful purpose
• local materials — materials found around the home or school, such as twigs and old cloth

## Worked examples

### Example 1
You have an old cotton shirt, a stick, sisal twine and a bucket. Which cleaning tools can you make?

Working:
1. The shirt can become a duster or part of a mop.
2. The stick and twine can hold a mop cloth or a twig broom.
3. The bucket can be a dustbin if it has or can be given a cover.

Answer: A duster or mop from the shirt and stick, and a dustbin from the bucket.

## Activity: Make one cleaning tool
You will need: Old cotton cloths, Sticks, Twine or string, Twigs or a bucket, Scissors used by the teacher or a careful learner
1. In groups, choose a broom, mop, duster or covered bin that you can make safely.
2. Make the tool with local materials and check that it is firm and clean.
3. Use it to sweep, dust, mop or collect refuse in the classroom area.
4. Wash or shake it, store it, and explain why your design works.

## Practice
1. Name two cleaning tools that can be made at home.
2. What makes an improvised duster unsuitable?
3. How should a homemade mop be cared for after use?

## Summary
• Brooms, mops, dusters and bins can be made from local materials.
• The tool must be clean, firm and safe to handle.
• Wash and dry improvised tools so they are ready to use again.

### Answers to practice
1. Any two: a twig broom, a cloth mop, a cloth duster, a dustpan from a tin or carton, a bucket dustbin.
2. Cloth that is oily, very dirty or falling to pieces, because it spreads dirt.
3. Wash it and dry it in the sun so that it does not stay sour.

PAGE 9: Lesson 8: Keeping the classroom clean every day

LESSON 8: KEEPING THE CLASSROOM CLEAN EVERY DAY
===============================================

## What you will learn
• Apply sweeping, dusting and refuse disposal in the classroom.
• Explain why a clean classroom is part of domestic hygiene.

Curriculum outcomes: c) appreciate a clean environment in promoting domestic hygiene

## Introduction
You spend most of the school day in one room. That room is a living environment. Crumbs, muddy shoes and an open dustbin change how pleasant and how healthy the day is.

## Notes
The classroom is cleaned with the same methods as a home. A daily routine keeps the work small. At the end of the day, or at the time your teacher sets, one group can sweep, one can dust, and one can empty the bin. Rotate the groups so that everyone learns every method and nobody feels the work belongs only to them.

Before sweeping, pick up paper and large rubbish. Sweep under desks. Dust the desks and the windowsill with damp cloths. Empty pencil sharpenings into the bin, not onto the floor. If the floor is cement and your teacher agrees, mop it on some days after sweeping. Let it dry before the next class sits down.

The class dustbin needs a lid and a daily empty. Sort what you can. Paper that is still clean on one side can be kept for rough work. Food waste should not stay in the bin over a hot weekend. Take it to the school compost or the proper disposal point.

During the day, hygiene is also about what you do not drop. Put wrappings in the bin when you finish a snack. Shake mud off your shoes at the door. Wipe a spill when it happens instead of walking through it. Open windows for fresh air, then close them if rain is blowing in.

A clean classroom helps to control communicable diseases because flies and dirt have fewer places to rest near your books and your food. It also makes the room a calmer place to learn. Appreciating that cleanliness means you leave the room better than you found it, even on a day when you are not in the duty group.

At home, use the same routine in the room where you sleep and do homework. The skill travels with you.

## Key words
• duty group — learners taking a turn to clean a shared place
• routine — a set of cleaning jobs done in order, day after day

## Worked examples

### Example 1
The class bin is full of peels and has no lid, and the floor under the desks was not swept. What should the duty group do?

Working:
1. Refuse should be emptied and the bin covered.
2. Sweeping must include the area under the desks.
3. Peels can go to compost if the school has a heap.

Answer: Empty and cover the bin, compost the peels if possible, and sweep under the desks as well as the open floor.

## Activity: Run a classroom cleaning routine
You will need: Brooms, Dust cloths, Dustbin with lid, Mop and bucket if the floor will be mopped, Duty list
1. Agree a duty list that rotates sweeping, dusting and refuse disposal.
2. Carry out today's jobs using the methods you have learnt.
3. Check under desks, on sills and inside the bin before you finish.
4. Write one reason you value a clean classroom and one job you will also do at home.

## Practice
1. Why should cleaning duties be rotated?
2. Name three classroom jobs that use the methods of this sub-strand.
3. How does a clean classroom help health?

## Summary
• Sweep, dust and empty the bin on a rotating duty list.
• Do not drop litter, and deal with spills at once.
• A clean classroom is part of caring for a shared living environment.

### Answers to practice
1. So that every learner practises each method and the work is shared fairly.
2. Sweeping the floor, dusting desks and disposing of refuse in the class bin.
3. It gives flies and dirt fewer places to rest near books and food, which helps control the spread of disease.

REVISION QUIZ — 3.2 DOMESTIC HYGIENE
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Which set lists methods of cleaning the home environment?
   A. Boiling, frying and baking
   B. Sweeping, dusting, mopping and disposal of refuse
   C. Weeding, pruning and harvesting
   D. Knitting, tacking and hemming

2. Why sprinkle a little water before sweeping a dusty room?
   A. To make the floor ready for painting
   B. To stop dust rising into the air
   C. To feed insects
   D. To replace mopping forever

3. How should furniture be dusted?

4. Why sweep before mopping?
   A. Mopping only works on carpets
   B. Loose dirt would be dragged through the water
   C. Soap cannot be used after sweeping
   D. The broom is washed in the mop bucket

5. Which waste can be composted?
   A. Polythene bags
   B. Broken glass
   C. Vegetable peels
   D. Old batteries

6. Why keep a separate mop for the latrine?

7. Why should tins of rainwater in the compound be emptied?
   A. To water the dustbin
   B. Because mosquitoes breed in standing water
   C. So the tins can be burnt
   D. Because rainwater is always dirty to touch

8. Which material can become a duster?
   A. A clean old cotton cloth
   B. Oily engine rags
   C. Broken glass
   D. A handful of thorns

9. What does a class duty list help learners to do?

10. How does domestic hygiene support health?
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 3.2 DOMESTIC HYGIENE
========================================

1. B. Sweeping, dusting, mopping and disposal of refuse
   These are the cleaning methods named for domestic hygiene.

2. B. To stop dust rising into the air
   A light sprinkle holds dust down so you do not breathe it or spread it.

3. With a slightly damp cloth, working from the top downwards.
   A damp cloth traps dust, and top-to-bottom order stops dust falling onto clean surfaces.

4. B. Loose dirt would be dragged through the water
   Sweeping removes loose rubbish so the mop can wash the floor instead of spreading waste.

5. C. Vegetable peels
   Vegetable peels rot and can become compost. Plastics, glass and batteries do not belong in compost.

6. So that germs from the latrine are not carried into the kitchen.
   Tools used on toilet floors should not then be used where food is prepared.

7. B. Because mosquitoes breed in standing water
   Standing water is a breeding place for mosquitoes.

8. A. A clean old cotton cloth
   Clean cotton holds dust. Oily or sharp materials are unsafe and spread dirt.

9. Share sweeping, dusting and refuse disposal fairly and practise each method.
   Rotation stops the work falling on one person and builds the habit of a clean room.

10. A clean home and classroom give flies, rats and germs fewer places to live near people and food.
   Removing dirt and refuse helps control communicable diseases.

studyPages.title: Overview
studyPages.body:
OVERVIEW
========

Domestic hygiene means keeping the home and the places you live in clean. In this sub-strand you will describe and use sweeping, dusting, mopping and proper disposal of refuse, make simple cleaning tools from local materials, and practise the same care in the classroom.

## Strand 3.0: Hygiene Practices
Sub-strand 3.2: Domestic Hygiene
Suggested lessons: 9

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) describe the various methods used for cleaning home environment
b) use appropriate methods to clean home environment
c) appreciate a clean environment in promoting domestic hygiene

## Key inquiry questions
1. How can we maintain hygiene in the home environment?

## Core competencies
• Creativity and imagination: thoughtful choices as learners use improvised and locally available cleaning resources.

## Values
• Responsibility: accountability as learners engage in activities of cleaning home environment.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Environmental awareness as learners maintain clean healthy environment.

## Links to other learning areas
• Learners relate clean environment to control of communicable diseases learnt in Science and Technology.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Agriculture Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 3.0 Hygiene Practices, Sub-strand 3.2 Domestic Hygiene

studyPages.title: Lesson 1: A clean home environment
studyPages.body:
LESSON 1: A CLEAN HOME ENVIRONMENT
==================================

## What you will learn
• Explain what domestic hygiene is.
• Name the main methods of cleaning the home environment.

Curriculum outcomes: a) describe the various methods used for cleaning home environment; c) appreciate a clean environment in promoting domestic hygiene

## Introduction
Food crumbs under a table, ash blown across the floor and a pile of peels by the door all invite flies and bad smells. Domestic hygiene is the work of keeping those things out of the place where people live.

## Notes
Domestic hygiene is the cleanliness of the home environment. The home environment includes the rooms, the kitchen, the compound, the latrine or toilet, and the place where animals are kept if it is close to the house. A clean environment protects the people who live there. Dirt, stagnant water and rotting refuse give germs, flies, rats and mosquitoes places to breed.

The methods you will use are sweeping, dusting, mopping and disposal of refuse. Sweeping removes loose dirt from floors and the compound with a broom. Dusting removes dust from furniture, windowsills and shelves with a cloth. Mopping washes floors after sweeping, using water and a mop or floor cloth. Disposal of refuse means collecting rubbish and putting it where it will not harm people, such as a covered dustbin, a compost pit or a proper waste pit.

Each method suits a type of dirt. Dry soil and scraps are swept. Fine dust on a desk is dusted. A sticky kitchen floor is mopped. Banana peels and paper are disposed of, not swept from one corner to another. Using the wrong method can make more mess. Dry-sweeping a very dusty room without care fills the air with dust that settles again. Mopping a floor that is still covered with rubbish only spreads the rubbish.

A clean home is more pleasant to sit, cook and sleep in. It also supports the personal hygiene you have already learnt. There is little point washing hands and then drying them on a filthy cloth, or cooking in a kitchen full of flies. Appreciating a clean environment means you notice dirt and you take a turn to remove it, at home and at school.

The same methods work in the classroom. Desks, the floor and the class dustbin are your home environment for many hours of the day.

## Key words
• domestic hygiene — keeping the home and its surroundings clean
• refuse — rubbish and waste that must be thrown away or composted
• home environment — the rooms, kitchen, compound and toilet where a family lives

## Worked examples

### Example 1
The kitchen floor has peels, spilled porridge and dust on the shelf. Which cleaning method fits each problem?

Working:
1. Peels are refuse and should be collected and disposed of.
2. Spilled porridge needs the floor washed after loose dirt is removed.
3. Dust on the shelf is removed by dusting.

Answer: Dispose of the peels, sweep then mop the floor, and dust the shelf.

## Activity: Discuss how a home is cleaned
You will need: Exercise book, Chalkboard
1. In groups, list the parts of a home that need cleaning.
2. Discuss which method you would use in each part: sweeping, dusting, mopping or disposal of refuse.
3. Give one reason a clean home protects health.
4. Share your list with another group and add any method you had missed.

## Practice
1. What is domestic hygiene?
2. Name the four cleaning methods in this sub-strand.
3. Why should refuse not be left in a corner of the kitchen?

## Summary
• Domestic hygiene keeps rooms, the kitchen, the compound and the toilet clean.
• The main methods are sweeping, dusting, mopping and disposing of refuse.
• Match the method to the kind of dirt.

### Answers to practice
1. Keeping the home environment clean.
2. Sweeping, dusting, mopping and disposal of refuse.
3. It smells, attracts flies and rats, and can spread disease.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Sweeping floors and the compound
studyPages.body:
LESSON 2: SWEEPING FLOORS AND THE COMPOUND
==========================================

## What you will learn
• Describe how to sweep a room and a compound.
• Sweep and collect dirt without spreading dust.

Curriculum outcomes: a) describe the various methods used for cleaning home environment; b) use appropriate methods to clean home environment

## Introduction
A broom looks simple, but a careless sweep sends dust into the air and leaves a ridge of dirt against the wall. Good sweeping collects the dirt in one place.

## Notes
Sweeping uses a broom to gather loose dirt. A soft broom suits a classroom or a cement floor inside the house. A twig broom or grass broom suits the compound and a rough floor. Hold the broom so that you can pull dirt towards you without bending only your back. Work from the far corner of the room towards the door, so you do not walk over the clean part.

If the floor is very dusty, sprinkle a little clean water first. The moisture holds the dust down so that you do not breathe a cloud of it. Do not soak the floor. That is mopping, and it comes later. Sweep under beds, tables and desks, not only the open middle of the room. Overlap each stroke so that strips of dirt are not left between them.

Gather the dirt into a small pile. Push it into a dustpan, a stiff piece of cardboard, or a tin cut to make a pan. Empty it into a dustbin with a lid. Do not sweep dirt out of the door and leave it on the step, and do not hide it under a mat. Dirt left at the doorway walks back in on people's feet.

In the compound, sweep leaves, feathers and litter into a pile. Collect them. Do not burn plastics with the leaves. Plant rubbish can go to a compost heap if you have learnt to make one. Standing water is not removed by a broom. Fill or drain puddles so that mosquitoes do not breed.

Shake the broom outside after use and hang it up. A broom left on a dirty floor stays dirty for the next sweep. Wash your hands when you finish.

## Key words
• sweeping — gathering loose dirt with a broom
• dustpan — a flat pan used to pick up a pile of swept dirt

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Why do you start sweeping at the far corner and move towards the door?

Working:
1. The dirt is pushed in one direction.
2. You finish at the exit and you do not step on the area you have just cleaned.

Answer: So that dirt moves towards the door and you do not walk over the clean floor.

## Activity: Sweep the classroom
You will need: Brooms, Dustpan, Dustbin with a lid, A little water in a cup for sprinkling
1. Move chairs carefully and sprinkle a little water if the floor is very dusty.
2. Sweep from the far corners towards the door, including under the desks.
3. Collect the dirt in a dustpan and empty it into the class dustbin.
4. Hang the brooms up and wash your hands.

## Practice
1. Why sprinkle a little water before sweeping a very dusty floor?
2. Where should swept dirt be put?
3. What should be done with a broom after sweeping?

## Summary
• Sweep from the far corner towards the door.
• Sprinkle a little water if dust would otherwise rise.
• Collect the dirt and empty it into a covered bin.

### Answers to practice
1. The water stops dust from rising into the air.
2. Into a dustbin, not left on the step or under a mat.
3. Shake it outside and hang it up.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Dusting furniture and surfaces
studyPages.body:
LESSON 3: DUSTING FURNITURE AND SURFACES
========================================

## What you will learn
• Describe the correct way to dust.
• Dust a desk or shelf without spreading dust.

Curriculum outcomes: a) describe the various methods used for cleaning home environment; b) use appropriate methods to clean home environment

## Introduction
Dust is fine and light. A dry flick of a cloth can lift it into the air so that it settles again on the same desk. Dusting should trap the dust, not move it around the room.

## Notes
Dusting cleans surfaces that a broom does not reach well: desks, tables, chairs, windowsills, shelves, window panes and the frames of pictures. The tool is a soft cloth. An old cotton cloth works better than a rough sack that scratches furniture.

Fold the cloth so that you have a clean side ready. For ordinary furniture, slightly dampen the cloth. The dampness holds dust instead of throwing it up. The cloth should be damp, not dripping. A dripping cloth leaves muddy streaks and can spoil books and paper. Keep water away from books, electrical switches and sockets.

Dust from the top downwards. Dust the shelf before the table under it, and the table before the legs and the floor. If you dust the low parts first, dust from above falls onto them again. Support a picture or a book with one hand while you dust with the other so that nothing falls.

Shake or rinse the cloth outside or over a basin when it is loaded with dust. Do not shake it beside a classmate's face. When the job is finished, wash the cloth and hang it to dry. A dirty duster spreads old dirt onto the next surface.

In the classroom, dusting comes after or before sweeping depending on what your teacher prefers, but the desk tops should be clear of books first so you are not wiping dirt into pages. Stack books neatly afterwards. Dusting the teacher's table and the windowsill is part of the same work, not a favour for one person.

Dust holds germs and makes a room look uncared for. A damp cloth and a top-to-bottom order are enough to do the job well.

## Key words
• dusting — removing fine dust from surfaces with a cloth
• damp cloth — a cloth that is slightly wet so that dust sticks to it

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner dusts the floor-level shelf first and the high window sill second, using a dry cloth that is shaken in the room. What should change?

Working:
1. High surfaces should be dusted before low ones.
2. A slightly damp cloth traps dust.
3. The cloth should be shaken outside, not in the room.

Answer: Use a slightly damp cloth, dust from top to bottom, and shake the cloth outside.

## Activity: Dust the classroom surfaces
You will need: Soft cotton cloths, A little clean water, Basin
1. Clear books off the desks.
2. Damp the cloths slightly and dust from the highest surfaces downwards.
3. Rinse or shake the cloths outside when they are dirty.
4. Wash and hang the cloths at the end, then wash your hands.

## Practice
1. Why is a slightly damp cloth better than a dry flick of cloth?
2. In what order should surfaces be dusted?
3. What must you keep water away from when dusting?

## Summary
• Use a slightly damp soft cloth.
• Dust from top to bottom.
• Wash the cloth afterwards and do not shake it in people's faces.

### Answers to practice
1. The damp cloth traps dust instead of throwing it into the air.
2. From the top downwards.
3. Books, paper and electrical switches or sockets.

studyPages.title: Lesson 4: Mopping floors
studyPages.body:
LESSON 4: MOPPING FLOORS
========================

## What you will learn
• Describe how to mop a floor.
• Mop a floor after it has been swept.

Curriculum outcomes: a) describe the various methods used for cleaning home environment; b) use appropriate methods to clean home environment

## Introduction
Sweeping takes away the loose dirt. Mopping takes away the film of dust and spills that a broom leaves behind. A kitchen or a cement classroom floor often needs both.

## Notes
Mopping is washing a floor with water and a mop or a strong floor cloth. Always sweep first. If you mop over stones, leaves and peels, you drag them across the floor and dirty the water at once.

You need a bucket, clean water, soap or detergent, and a mop. A mop can be a shop mop or a thick cloth tied firmly to a stick. Put a little soap in the water so that grease can lift. Dip the mop, then wring it hard. A dripping mop floods the floor, makes it slippery, and takes a long time to dry. The mop should be damp.

Work in sections from the far side of the room towards the door. Overlap the sections. Rinse the mop when it looks dirty, and change the water when it turns grey. Mopping with dirty water only paints the dirt back on. Pay attention to corners and to the area under the table where spills dry.

Leave the floor to dry before people walk on it. Wet cement and tiles are slippery, and wet dust sticks to shoes. Open a window if you can so that the floor dries faster. Do not mop electrical cords or sockets.

In a kitchen, mop after cooking when spills of porridge, milk or oil are still easy to lift. Grease needs soap, not water alone. In a latrine with a cement floor, mopping with soapy water and a separate mop keeps smells down. Do not use the kitchen mop in the latrine. Germs would travel back to the cooking area.

Empty the bucket away from the drinking-water source. Hang the mop to dry so that it does not stay sour. Wash your hands.

## Key words
• mopping — washing a floor with a damp mop or floor cloth and soapy water
• wring — to twist a mop or cloth to squeeze out extra water

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Why should the kitchen mop not be used to clean the latrine?

Working:
1. The latrine floor has germs from human waste.
2. The same mop would carry those germs into the kitchen.

Answer: Germs from the latrine would be spread where food is prepared.

## Activity: Mop a swept floor
You will need: Bucket, Clean water, Soap, Mop or floor cloth tied to a stick, Broom
1. Sweep the chosen floor first and remove the loose dirt.
2. Mix a little soap in a bucket of clean water and wring the mop until it is damp.
3. Mop from the far side towards the door, changing the water when it is dirty.
4. Leave the floor to dry, empty the bucket in a safe place, hang the mop, and wash your hands.

## Practice
1. Why do you sweep before you mop?
2. Why should a mop be wrung out?
3. What should you do when the mop water turns grey?
4. Where should you empty dirty mop water?

## Summary
• Sweep first, then mop with a well-wrung mop and soapy water.
• Change dirty water and let the floor dry.
• Keep the latrine mop separate from the kitchen mop.

### Answers to practice
1. So that loose rubbish is not dragged through the wash water.
2. A dripping mop floods the floor and makes it slippery.
3. Change it for clean soapy water.
4. Away from the drinking-water source.

studyPages.title: Lesson 5: Disposal of refuse
studyPages.body:
LESSON 5: DISPOSAL OF REFUSE
============================

## What you will learn
• Sort household refuse.
• Dispose of each kind of refuse in a safe way.

Curriculum outcomes: a) describe the various methods used for cleaning home environment; b) use appropriate methods to clean home environment

## Introduction
A dustbin that is never emptied is just a smell with a lid. Disposal means the rubbish leaves the living area and goes somewhere it will not harm people, water or animals.

## Notes
Refuse is the waste a home throws away: food peels, ash, sweepings, paper, plastics, tins, broken glass and worn-out items. Leaving it in the compound attracts flies, rats and dogs, and rain can wash it into a well or a river.

Sort refuse before you dispose of it. Food remains, peels, leaves and other plant waste can rot. These belong on a compost heap or in a compost pit, where they become manure, as you learnt when studying soil. Ash from clean wood can also go into compost in small amounts. Do not put plastics, glass or metal in the compost.

Paper and dry leaves should not be mixed with food waste if you can help it. Plastics, tins and bottles should be kept in a separate container so they can be collected or reused. Do not burn plastics. The smoke is harmful to breathe. Broken glass must be wrapped or placed in a strong container so that it does not cut the person who handles the rubbish.

Use a dustbin with a lid in the kitchen and the classroom. Empty it every day. A bin without a lid feeds flies. If your area has a collection point or a county collection day, take the non-rotting waste there. If it does not, use a proper waste pit dug away from the house and away from the water source, and cover fresh refuse with soil. Do not use the river, the road or the school hedge as a dump.

Wear gloves or use a stick and a dustpan when you handle refuse. Wash your hands afterwards. Rinse the dustbin sometimes so that it does not smell even when it is empty.

Good disposal is part of cleaning. Sweeping and mopping move dirt. Disposal makes sure the dirt does not come back.

## Key words
• disposal — putting waste in a safe place away from where people live
• sort — to separate waste into types so each type is handled correctly
• waste pit — a pit, away from water sources, where refuse is buried

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Sort these items: mango peels, a polythene bag, broken glass, dry leaves from the sweep.

Working:
1. Mango peels can rot and can go to compost.
2. Dry leaves can go to compost if they are not mixed with plastic.
3. A polythene bag does not rot and should be kept with other plastics.
4. Broken glass must be handled so that it does not cut anyone.

Answer: Compost the peels and the leaves. Keep the polythene bag separate. Wrap or box the glass and put it with non-rotting waste.

## Activity: Sort and empty the class refuse
You will need: Dustbin, Gloves or a dustpan and stick, Compost area if the school has one, Water and soap
1. Empty the class bin onto a safe surface and sort rotting waste from plastics and other rubbish.
2. Take plant waste to the compost if your teacher has one, and bag or bin the rest for proper disposal.
3. Wash or line the class bin and fit the lid.
4. Wash your hands with soap.

## Practice
1. Which refuse can go on a compost heap?
2. Why should plastics not be burnt in the compound?
3. Why does a dustbin need a lid?

## Summary
• Sort rotting waste from plastics, tins and glass.
• Compost plant waste and put other refuse in a covered bin or a proper pit.
• Never dump refuse in rivers or roads, and wash your hands after handling it.

### Answers to practice
1. Plant and food waste that can rot, such as peels and leaves, not plastics, glass or metal.
2. The smoke is harmful to breathe.
3. A lid keeps out flies and stops the smell and the rubbish from spreading.

studyPages.title: Lesson 6: Cleaning the kitchen, compound and latrine
studyPages.body:
LESSON 6: CLEANING THE KITCHEN, COMPOUND AND LATRINE
====================================================

## What you will learn
• Choose the right method for each part of the home.
• Describe a simple cleaning order for a kitchen and a latrine.

Curriculum outcomes: b) use appropriate methods to clean home environment

## Introduction
A home is not one surface. The kitchen, the compound and the latrine get dirty in different ways, so a useful clean follows a different order in each place.

## Notes
In the kitchen, start by picking up refuse and scraping food off utensils. Sort the refuse. Wash utensils with soap and clean water, rinse them, and spread them to dry on a rack, not on the floor. Then dust shelves. Sweep the floor. Mop last, with the kitchen mop. Cover water and food before you begin so that dust does not settle in them. Wipe the table where food is prepared with a clean cloth and soapy water.

Keep animals out of the kitchen. A goat or a chicken brings droppings and flies to the place where food is kept. Store utensils upside down or in a closed cupboard so that dust does not collect inside cups.

In the compound, pick up litter first. Sweep paths and the area around the door. Cut long grass near the house if that is your family task, because mosquitoes rest in it. Tip out tins and old tyres that hold rainwater. Those small pools breed mosquitoes. Check that the compost or waste pit is not spilling back into the yard. A compound clean-up is mostly sweeping, picking refuse and removing standing water. Mopping the soil is not useful.

For a latrine or toilet, sweep the floor, then mop with soapy water using a mop that stays in that place. Scrub the slab or seat with a brush and soapy water. Keep ash or other materials your family uses for the pit, but do not throw rubbish such as plastics into the pit. A latrine cover or a tight door keeps flies down. Wash your hands at the station next to the latrine when you leave. Never eat while you are cleaning it.

Do these jobs often. A kitchen wiped every day is easier than a kitchen left for a week. Share the work so that one person is not always the only cleaner.

## Key words
• latrine — a toilet, often a pit toilet, used at home or school
• standing water — water left sitting in tins, tyres or puddles

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Put these kitchen jobs in a sensible order: mop, wash utensils, pick up peels, sweep.

Working:
1. Refuse is removed first so it is not washed around.
2. Utensils are washed before the floor, or they drip on a clean floor.
3. Sweeping comes before mopping.

Answer: Pick up peels, wash utensils, sweep, then mop.

## Activity: Plan a clean for three places
You will need: Exercise book, Manila paper
1. In groups, choose the kitchen, the compound or the latrine.
2. Write the methods you will use, in order, and the tools you need.
3. Include one safety or hygiene rule, such as a separate mop or washing hands.
4. Present the plan and let the class add anything important that is missing.

## Practice
1. Why should food be covered before you sweep the kitchen?
2. Why should tins holding rainwater be tipped out?
3. What is special about the mop used in the latrine?

## Summary
• In the kitchen, remove refuse, wash utensils, dust, sweep and mop.
• In the compound, collect litter, sweep and remove standing water.
• Clean the latrine with its own tools and wash your hands afterwards.

### Answers to practice
1. So that dust from sweeping does not fall into the food.
2. Mosquitoes breed in standing water.
3. It should be kept for the latrine only, not used in the kitchen.

studyPages.title: Lesson 7: Cleaning tools from local materials
studyPages.body:
LESSON 7: CLEANING TOOLS FROM LOCAL MATERIALS
=============================================

## What you will learn
• Make or name simple cleaning tools from local materials.
• Use improvised tools to keep a place clean.

Curriculum outcomes: b) use appropriate methods to clean home environment; c) appreciate a clean environment in promoting domestic hygiene

## Introduction
A shop mop is useful, but it is not the only mop. Many homes already make brooms from twigs, dusters from old cotton and dustbins from tins. Good cleaning uses what you can find, as long as it does the job safely.

## Notes
Improvised tools are tools you make from materials around you. They support domestic hygiene when bought equipment is not at hand.

A broom can be made by tying a bundle of suitable twigs, coconut-leaf spines or long grass firmly onto a stick. The tying must be tight so that pieces do not fall out while you sweep. A dustpan can be cut from a clean plastic container or a firm cardboard box. A duster can be an old cotton T-shirt washed and hemmed roughly so that it does not fray onto the furniture. A mop can be several thick cotton cloths tied securely to a stick. A dustbin can be a bucket with a fitted cover, or a sack hung on a nail for dry paper only. A cover can be a piece of wood or a lid from another container.

Choose materials that can be cleaned. A duster made from a cloth that is already oily spreads grease. A bin made from a leaking tin spreads dirty water. Glass and sharp metal edges must be covered or avoided so that nobody is cut while cleaning.

Local does not mean careless. An improvised broom used every day is better than a fine broom left unused. After use, shake brooms, wash cloths and mop heads, and stand them in the sun to dry. Replace a broom when the twigs are too short to gather dirt.

In class, groups can make one tool and use it the same week. Label the latrine mop if you make one, so that it is not taken to the kitchen. Creativity here is a practical choice: you look at what is available and you make a tool that sweeps, dusts, mops or holds refuse.

Appreciating a clean environment includes being willing to invent the tool that keeps it clean.

## Key words
• improvised — made from materials you already have, for a useful purpose
• local materials — materials found around the home or school, such as twigs and old cloth

## Worked examples

### Example 1
You have an old cotton shirt, a stick, sisal twine and a bucket. Which cleaning tools can you make?

Working:
1. The shirt can become a duster or part of a mop.
2. The stick and twine can hold a mop cloth or a twig broom.
3. The bucket can be a dustbin if it has or can be given a cover.

Answer: A duster or mop from the shirt and stick, and a dustbin from the bucket.

## Activity: Make one cleaning tool
You will need: Old cotton cloths, Sticks, Twine or string, Twigs or a bucket, Scissors used by the teacher or a careful learner
1. In groups, choose a broom, mop, duster or covered bin that you can make safely.
2. Make the tool with local materials and check that it is firm and clean.
3. Use it to sweep, dust, mop or collect refuse in the classroom area.
4. Wash or shake it, store it, and explain why your design works.

## Practice
1. Name two cleaning tools that can be made at home.
2. What makes an improvised duster unsuitable?
3. How should a homemade mop be cared for after use?

## Summary
• Brooms, mops, dusters and bins can be made from local materials.
• The tool must be clean, firm and safe to handle.
• Wash and dry improvised tools so they are ready to use again.

### Answers to practice
1. Any two: a twig broom, a cloth mop, a cloth duster, a dustpan from a tin or carton, a bucket dustbin.
2. Cloth that is oily, very dirty or falling to pieces, because it spreads dirt.
3. Wash it and dry it in the sun so that it does not stay sour.

studyPages.title: Lesson 8: Keeping the classroom clean every day
studyPages.body:
LESSON 8: KEEPING THE CLASSROOM CLEAN EVERY DAY
===============================================

## What you will learn
• Apply sweeping, dusting and refuse disposal in the classroom.
• Explain why a clean classroom is part of domestic hygiene.

Curriculum outcomes: c) appreciate a clean environment in promoting domestic hygiene

## Introduction
You spend most of the school day in one room. That room is a living environment. Crumbs, muddy shoes and an open dustbin change how pleasant and how healthy the day is.

## Notes
The classroom is cleaned with the same methods as a home. A daily routine keeps the work small. At the end of the day, or at the time your teacher sets, one group can sweep, one can dust, and one can empty the bin. Rotate the groups so that everyone learns every method and nobody feels the work belongs only to them.

Before sweeping, pick up paper and large rubbish. Sweep under desks. Dust the desks and the windowsill with damp cloths. Empty pencil sharpenings into the bin, not onto the floor. If the floor is cement and your teacher agrees, mop it on some days after sweeping. Let it dry before the next class sits down.

The class dustbin needs a lid and a daily empty. Sort what you can. Paper that is still clean on one side can be kept for rough work. Food waste should not stay in the bin over a hot weekend. Take it to the school compost or the proper disposal point.

During the day, hygiene is also about what you do not drop. Put wrappings in the bin when you finish a snack. Shake mud off your shoes at the door. Wipe a spill when it happens instead of walking through it. Open windows for fresh air, then close them if rain is blowing in.

A clean classroom helps to control communicable diseases because flies and dirt have fewer places to rest near your books and your food. It also makes the room a calmer place to learn. Appreciating that cleanliness means you leave the room better than you found it, even on a day when you are not in the duty group.

At home, use the same routine in the room where you sleep and do homework. The skill travels with you.

## Key words
• duty group — learners taking a turn to clean a shared place
• routine — a set of cleaning jobs done in order, day after day

## Worked examples

### Example 1
The class bin is full of peels and has no lid, and the floor under the desks was not swept. What should the duty group do?

Working:
1. Refuse should be emptied and the bin covered.
2. Sweeping must include the area under the desks.
3. Peels can go to compost if the school has a heap.

Answer: Empty and cover the bin, compost the peels if possible, and sweep under the desks as well as the open floor.

## Activity: Run a classroom cleaning routine
You will need: Brooms, Dust cloths, Dustbin with lid, Mop and bucket if the floor will be mopped, Duty list
1. Agree a duty list that rotates sweeping, dusting and refuse disposal.
2. Carry out today's jobs using the methods you have learnt.
3. Check under desks, on sills and inside the bin before you finish.
4. Write one reason you value a clean classroom and one job you will also do at home.

## Practice
1. Why should cleaning duties be rotated?
2. Name three classroom jobs that use the methods of this sub-strand.
3. How does a clean classroom help health?

## Summary
• Sweep, dust and empty the bin on a rotating duty list.
• Do not drop litter, and deal with spills at once.
• A clean classroom is part of caring for a shared living environment.

### Answers to practice
1. So that every learner practises each method and the work is shared fairly.
2. Sweeping the floor, dusting desks and disposing of refuse in the class bin.
3. It gives flies and dirt fewer places to rest near books and food, which helps control the spread of disease.

questions.question: Which set lists methods of cleaning the home environment?
options: Sweeping, dusting, mopping and disposal of refuse
questions.explanation: These are the cleaning methods named for domestic hygiene.

questions.question: Why sprinkle a little water before sweeping a dusty room?
options: To make the floor ready for painting
To stop dust rising into the air
questions.explanation: A light sprinkle holds dust down so you do not breathe it or spread it.

questions.question: How should furniture be dusted?
questions.answer: With a slightly damp cloth, working from the top downwards.
questions.explanation: A damp cloth traps dust, and top-to-bottom order stops dust falling onto clean surfaces.

questions.question: Why sweep before mopping?
options: Loose dirt would be dragged through the water
Soap cannot be used after sweeping
The broom is washed in the mop bucket
questions.explanation: Sweeping removes loose rubbish so the mop can wash the floor instead of spreading waste.

questions.question: Which waste can be composted?
questions.explanation: Vegetable peels rot and can become compost. Plastics, glass and batteries do not belong in compost.

questions.question: Why keep a separate mop for the latrine?
questions.answer: So that germs from the latrine are not carried into the kitchen.
questions.explanation: Tools used on toilet floors should not then be used where food is prepared.

questions.question: Why should tins of rainwater in the compound be emptied?
options: Because mosquitoes breed in standing water
So the tins can be burnt
Because rainwater is always dirty to touch
questions.explanation: Standing water is a breeding place for mosquitoes.

questions.question: Which material can become a duster?
questions.explanation: Clean cotton holds dust. Oily or sharp materials are unsafe and spread dirt.

questions.question: What does a class duty list help learners to do?
questions.answer: Share sweeping, dusting and refuse disposal fairly and practise each method.
questions.explanation: Rotation stops the work falling on one person and builds the habit of a clean room.

questions.question: How does domestic hygiene support health?
questions.answer: A clean home and classroom give flies, rats and germs fewer places to live near people and food.
questions.explanation: Removing dirt and refuse helps control communicable diseases.
